body_markdown:
If you’ve been around the car hobby long enough, you’ve picked up a lot of “word of mouth” knowledge that comes from enthusiasts who’ve been around longer than you. Before the internet, it was only your family members, older car guys and gals, magazines, library books, and your own experimentation that were the fount of all automotive knowledge. Wisdom, along with some gross misconceptions, was passed along in quiet conversations under open hoods in darkened garages around the globe.


Now we have the internet, where about half of what you read is wrong or misstated, and online forum contributors don’t have an editor filtering out the hogwash. But even before the massive information interconnectivity that we now enjoy on the web, lots of old wives’ tales were passed down from generation to generation in the automotive world. Many still exist and are sometimes amplified by their repetition.


The great Keith Duckworth, co-founder of Cosworth, had many noble sayings, one of which was, “I’d rather be uninformed than misinformed.”


To that end, I’d like to start a short series on some common myths and demystify some of the science behind why they are wrong. Let’s start with bigger brakes.


## “Bigger Brakes Make You Stop Faster”


This first one is a bit counterintuitive. Almost every enthusiast would prefer larger brake calipers for the apparently sound reasoning that bigger pads and more pad contact equals more braking power. Sadly, science does not agree. Using a larger brake pad will not change the braking force one iota. It doesn’t sound correct, but that’s how it is.


Norman Garrett


The science: Let’s start with the force of friction created by a pad on a disc, as found in most cars today. The pad is pressed upon by a piston, which responds to hydraulic pressure on its backside (around 2000 psi at max pedal effort). The force of the piston pushes the brake pad against the brake rotor and tries to stop the rotor’s rotation by the clamping force of the pads on either side of the disc.


Let’s get technical. The amount of “stopping” torque created by the opposing pads on one rotor is driven by a simple equation for frictional force:


Where F is the frictional force, the Greek letter mu stands for the friction coefficient, and N is the normal force pushing the friction material into the corresponding surface (e.g., the brake pad being pressed into a rotating disc). The frictional force F creates a torque on the wheel hub through the structure of the rotor.


For a given normal force and a given friction coefficient, making the brake pad larger just spreads out the piston’s normal force across a larger area. This makes the “per square inch” pad pressure go down, and theoretically you may even experience less braking performance.


Think of a snowshoe versus a stiletto high-heeled shoe on snow. One floats on top of the snow (in the right conditions) since the person’s weight is spread out over a large area—the “per square inch” load is widely distributed and has been greatly reduced in comparison to the high-heeled shoe. The less force per square inch works in a snowshoe—with a larger brake pad, it only reduces the “incremental-area pressure” of the pad against the rotor.


Norman Garrett


Back to the formula: A larger brake pad does not increase the braking torque; it does not change the “N” in the force equation (it only changes the brake-pad-to-rotor psi number), so the force “F” is unchanged. This same argument can be made for larger tires and road traction, but that is another (much more complicated) discussion.


However, a larger brake *rotor* will create more braking power. This comes from more braking torque via a longer moment-arm (aka lever) from the pad to the center of rotation of the wheel hub. In the case of larger rotors, braking performance will be improved by “bigger brakes,” but not because of the size of the pads.


Norman Garrett


However #2: More pistons in the caliper make the normal force N more uniform across the pads’ faces. A single piston pushing on the center of a brake pad inevitably results in less pad pressure at the ends of the pad due to pad backing plate deflection. This is why more pistons in a can caliper improve braking: the average normal force N across the pad face is closer to what the piston(s) are applying to the backing plate of the pad assembly. Back to the pressure equation: More pistons mean the same brake fluid pressure is spread out over more piston area, so the effective normal force “N” goes down—more line pressure is needed. It becomes a complicated balancing act.


In practice, the leading edge tends to “jam” into the rotor (think of a paint scraper). Also, the part of the pad directly behind the piston, as you would expect, gets a lot of pressure applied to the rotor. As you move to the trailing edge of the pad (with respect to the rotor’s direction of rotation), the force tapers off. Since friction causes heat, you can see that the temperature across the brake pad’s face is all over the place as it experiences the leading-edge binding, the piston’s hard push in the center, and the lazy trailing edge. A brake pad can have localized fading in zones across its face during heavy braking. The best calipers have small pistons behind the leading edge of the pad and increasingly larger pistons as you move to the rear of the pad.


Norman Garrett


We only have three dials to turn to improve braking performance: Increase the normal force N; increase the coefficient of friction; or increase the moment-arm (leverage) through which the force acts upon the wheel hub.


So, larger brakes work when “larger” means bigger-diameter rotors giving a larger lever for the force to act on. And “larger” brakes work when a caliper gets more effective piston area, so each remote section of the brake pad face can apply a normal force closest to what the piston is trying to impart into the pad itself. The downside of all this? More unsprung mass (which your springs and dampers might not like) and more thermal mass to hold in the heat (but larger rotors have more surface area to reject heat from—once again, it gets complicated). If you want to be pedantic, the larger, heavier rotors take more engine power to accelerate, so they theoretically will make your car slower in acceleration… Like everything, it all is part of an interrelated system.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


When are larger pads beneficial? In reducing brake fade, which is an unavoidable phenomenon of any braking system (given our current tech). Brake fade is a function of pad temperature, which itself is tied to pad contact area. Most of us have felt brake fade at some point or another—it sometimes actually feels like the car is accelerating because you are expecting *some* increase in G forces from slamming on the brake pedal. My old ’64 Imperial had Class 5 truck drum brakes on it from the factory (i.e., a 3-ton car with 10-ton-rated truck brakes all around), and it stopped on a dime from 70 mph—once. Try it a second time within one minute and the pad material’s μ would go from ~0.30 to squishy pedal pretty quickly. Drum brakes trap a lot of heat; thus the change to disc brakes on front wheels starting in the ’60s and ’70s (with front discs first, since your front tires do about 60% of the braking due to weight transfer). Disc brake rotors are open to the air and cool off much better.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Lots of undesirable things happen when brake pad material gets hot, and “hot” means approaching 1000°F and higher in racing conditions. Road Atlanta has 12 turns, and a good lap time for a street car is about a minute and 40 seconds. There’s not much time for brakes to cool off, and fading eventually sets in on street pads. I remember testing street-trim sports cars on rented race tracks back in the day, and some cars would not make it around one lap before the brakes faded away.


[Eddy Eckart](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eeckarthagerty-com/)


As mentioned a few paragraphs earlier, the localized heating (and thus fading) across the pad face is highly variable, so racing applications can actually see improved braking performance from larger brake pads due to the thermal benefits. Larger brake pads spread the heat out over a larger surface area. They do improve brake *fade* performance, and that does lead to faster lap times.


Larger rotors require a new caliper mated to them, so the assembly gives you better braking (especially if the new caliper has multiple pistons and a larger pad to dissipate heat).


But wait, there is yet another variable. At some point, the tire locks up, and the brakes become meaningless. It could be argued that if you can lock up your front tires at 80 mph, you don’t need better brakes (unless you’re racing at 80+ mph…). In cars with ABS systems, how the ABS engagement point is calibrated determines your ultimate stopping power, regardless of pad size (and let’s add tires into the equation for that calibration…)


Norman Garrett


Higher-friction coefficients are always desirable, but often come with compromises such as poor cold-temperature performance, high noise or wear, etc. Most street pads have a μ of around 0.3 to 0.35. Race pads can exceed 0.5 in certain conditions. Pads are made for a chosen range of performance, sort of like how tires are built for a purpose, be it snow or hot-weather racing. Again, back to the varying pressures across the pad face, the frictional coefficient also varies across the face, and even changes zone-to-zone during a single braking event, since µ is tied closely to temperature, and temperature is closely tied to localized pad pressure and rotor speed. Caveat emptor: Published μ values from brake manufacturers are about as reliable as horsepower claims in the sixties and hair-restoration balm ads.


Like almost all things in engineering, it all gets rather complicated in actual practice.


But, at the core: Bigger brakes being better? It depends on what is bigger, but the size of the pad itself is not in the picture.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)
